extracted.intended_audience: immigration attorneys, advocacy groups, policymakers, regulated applicants, and members of the public preparing comments on the DHS public charge proposed rule
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the criteria, methodologies, and disclosure standards DHS used in the economic analysis and rule text of the proposed public charge regulation, to inform comments and evaluation of impacts. Includes statutory factors for public-charge determinations, cost estimation conventions, assumptions, and regulatory-flexibility considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors for public-charge determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires DHS to consider the following minimum factors that reflect the likelihood that an alien will become a public charge: the alien’s age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition, DHS may consider any affidavit of support submitted by the alien's sponsor and any other factors relevant to the likelihood of the alien becoming a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of support and other relevant factors
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS may consider any affidavit of support submitted by the alien’s sponsor and any other factors relevant to the likelihood of the alien becoming a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is explicitly in addition to the statutory minimum factors (age, health, family status, assets/resources/financial status, education/skills) and may affect determinations under the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary disenrollment/foregone-enrollment rate (2.5% baseline)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS uses a 2.5 percent rate of disenrollment or foregone enrollment as the baseline estimate for projecting reductions in transfer payments due to the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS multiplies the average annual benefit per person by the population likely to disenroll or forego enrollment to estimate transfer-payment reductions; DHS explicitly solicits comments on the methodology for estimating this rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity analysis using proximity-to-application (1- to 3-year windows)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS conducts a sensitivity analysis examining effects if prospective adjustment applicants disenroll or forego enrollment at least 36 months (3 years) in advance, producing population and transfer-payment ranges (e.g., 333,239 to 999,717 people; $1.51 billion to $4.53 billion reductions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS treats the 1-year estimate as the primary estimate for analysis but requests comment on whether the 3-year estimate is more appropriate; acknowledges individuals may alter behavior earlier due to heavy weighting of benefits within 36 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of federal transfer payments; treatment of state share
rubrics_metrics.description: The economic analysis estimates reductions in transfer payments paid by the federal government and notes potential additional reductions from state transfer payments, which DHS is often unable to fully quantify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where DHS does present state-level impacts it assumes the state share of federal financial participation (FFP) is 50 percent; DHS requests comments on additional sources of transfer payments and notes FMAP and state participation vary by program and state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specific program-level data and limits (Medicaid/SNAP/LIS/Security programs)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS uses program-specific per-enrollee benefit data (e.g., Medicaid, SNAP, Medicare LIS, SSI, TANF, Federal Rental Assistance) to estimate reductions but notes limitations, such as inability to disaggregate emergency vs. non-emergency Medicaid and variation in per-enrollee costs by eligibility group and state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimates may understate total transfer payments because average annual benefits per person may not include program administrative overhead; DHS cites program guidance as sources and flags heterogeneity across beneficiaries and states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discounting conventions: 3% and 7% discount rates over a 10-year horizon
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS applies 3 percent and 7 percent discount rates to compare costs over time and presents undiscounted and discounted totals over a 10-year period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables present annual costs, 10-year totals, and totals discounted at 3% and 7%; DHS welcomes comments on the choice of discounting and timelines used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of costs: direct costs and reduced transfer payments
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS separates quantified impacts into direct costs (e.g., filing, opportunity cost of time, costs from RFEs, public charge bond costs) and reduced transfer payments to the government resulting from disenrollment/foregone enrollment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each category is quantified (undiscounted and discounted) where feasible; DHS acknowledges some costs are not quantifiable and lists them as unquantified/indirect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific forms and cost components to include in direct-cost estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS presents and quantifies costs associated with specific forms and processes: Form I-944 (Declaration of Self-Sufficiency), opportunity cost of time for Forms I-485, I-129, I-129CW, I-539, costs for beneficiaries who receive RFEs to complete and submit Form I-944 (including opportunity cost of time and credit report/score costs), Form I-945 (public charge bond), and Form I-356 (cancellation of public charge bond).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS provides annual and 10-year cost ranges for each form and totals; notes uncertainty where RFEs and discretionary RFE issuance make some estimates imprecise and requests comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation of time: opportunity cost of time using average total compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS values the time burden (opportunity cost of time) using average total compensation figures (example given: $35.78 per hour) multiplied by estimated hours per task (e.g., 8–10 hours to read the rule; 1 hour for Form I-864W).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS uses these valuations to convert time burdens into dollar measures and includes these in direct-cost estimates; DHS documents data sources for time and wage estimates and solicits comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarization cost estimation (8–10 hours per person)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS estimates the time necessary to read and understand the rule is approximately 8 to 10 hours per person, and treats such time as an opportunity cost (direct cost to those regulated and indirect for others who choose to read it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entities (e.g., non-profits, advocacy groups) may have multiple persons incurring that time; DHS counts time for those directly regulated as direct costs and for others as indirect costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-monetized potential consequences to list and consider
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS enumerates primary non-monetized potential consequences of disenrollment or foregoing public benefits: worse health outcomes (including increased obesity/malnutrition, reduced prescription adherence), increased emergency-room use, increased prevalence of communicable diseases (including risk to U.S. citizens who are unvaccinated), increases in uncompensated care, increased poverty and housing instability, and reduced productivity and educational attainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS acknowledges other unanticipated consequences and requests public comments on additional possible consequences and methodologies for quantifying these non-monetized impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of OMB guidance for transfer-payment treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS references OMB Circular A-4 in discussing transfer payments and adheres to standard definitions and treatment where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The citation signals reliance on OMB guidance for economic-accounting treatment; DHS still notes program peculiarities (e.g., SNAP federal funding of food expenses but only partial admin cost coverage) that affect transfer-payment accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation conventions: undiscounted and discounted annual and 10-year totals
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS presents annual costs and transfers and aggregates them into 10-year totals, showing undiscounted amounts and amounts discounted at 3% and 7%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary tables (e.g., Tables 52–56) provide breakout by program and category; DHS uses these presentation conventions to facilitate public review and comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about limitations and unverifiable items
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS explicitly states limitations where it cannot quantify impacts (e.g., unable to determine exact number of RFEs requiring Form I-944, unable to disaggregate certain Medicaid expenditures, not readily able to track state funds), and labels such items as unquantified or uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS invites public comment to improve estimation methods and to identify additional sources of costs or transfer payments that could be quantified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) analysis requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the RFA, DHS must consider the potential impact of regulations on small businesses, small governmental jurisdictions, and small organizations; DHS conducts an Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) where provisions would directly regulate small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS identifies potentially affected small entities (e.g., petitioners who file Form I-129 or I-129CW and obligors that might request bond cancellation), quantifies increased time burdens (e.g., additional 30 minutes for petitioners filing I-129/I-129CW), and estimates associated costs; DHS requests comments on impacts to small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate increased time burden for petitioners (I-129/I-129CW) and resulting costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule increases the time burden by an additional 30 minutes on petitioners who file Form I-129 or Form I-129CW on behalf of a beneficiary requesting an extension of stay or change of status; DHS estimates population sizes and monetizes the opportunity-cost increase (e.g., about $184 million for Form I-129 beneficiaries and about $5 million for Form I-129CW beneficiaries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS uses its population estimates (e.g., annual beneficiary populations) and wage/time assumptions to calculate total costs and reports these in the IRFA and cost tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of filing fees as proxy for USCIS resource costs
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS establishes fees by assigning costs to an adjudication based on adjudication burden and use of USCIS resources; DHS treats the fee associated with an information collection as a reasonable measure of the collection’s costs to USCIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when a specific form does not charge a fee (e.g., I-693, I-864 series, I-912), DHS captures the cost to USCIS in the fee for the underlying benefit request; DHS welcomes comments on government-cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for public charge bond benefits and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS estimates costs associated with establishing/modifying a public charge bond process (Forms I-945 and I-356) and notes a potential benefit: allowing an immigrant opportunity to be admitted despite being likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS quantifies bond-related filing and opportunity costs where feasible and solicits comment on the net benefits of such a bond process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation of public comment on methods, assumptions, and unquantified impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the analysis DHS explicitly invites public comments on the estimation methodologies (e.g., disenrollment rates), choice of primary estimate (1-year vs. 3-year), discounting, inclusion/measurement of additional transfer payments, unquantified costs, and other assumptions used in the economic analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS identifies specific areas where comment is welcome and frames its estimates as preliminary and subject to change based on public input and better data.
